claim: ATAD1 (in humans; Msp1 in yeast) removes mislocalized membrane proteins from the mitochondrial outer membrane.
source: The mitochondrial AAA (ATPase Associated with diverse cellular Activities) protein ATAD1 (in humans; Msp1 in yeast) removes mislocalized membrane proteins, as well as stuck import substrates from the mitochondrial outer membrane, facilitating their re-insertion into their cognate organelles and maintaining mitochondria's protein import capacity.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is a well-established function of ATAD1/Msp1 supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: ATAD1 removes stuck import substrates from the mitochondrial outer membrane.
source: The mitochondrial AAA (ATPase Associated with diverse cellular Activities) protein ATAD1 (in humans; Msp1 in yeast) removes mislocalized membrane proteins, as well as stuck import substrates from the mitochondrial outer membrane, facilitating their re-insertion into their cognate organelles and maintaining mitochondria's protein import capacity.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: ATAD1 helps maintain proteostasis in mitochondria.
source: In doing so, it helps to maintain proteostasis in mitochondria.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a consequence of ATAD1's function.

claim: Msp1 utilizes multiple aromatic amino acids to firmly grip the substrate in the central pore.
source: Among these features in Msp1 was the utilization of multiple aromatic amino acids to firmly grip the substrate in the central pore.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by previous structural work (Wang et al., 2020).

claim: The cryo-EM structures of human ATAD1 in complex with a peptide substrate were determined at near atomic resolution.
source: In this work, we determined the cryo-EM structures of the human ATAD1 in complex with a peptide substrate at near atomic resolution.
evidence: This is the primary experimental result of the study, with structures resolved at 3.2 Å and 3.5 Å.

claim: Phylogenetically conserved structural elements adapt ATAD1 for its function.
source: The structures show that phylogenetically conserved structural elements adapt ATAD1 for its function while generally adopting a conserved mechanism shared by many AAA proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural comparisons throughout the manuscript.

claim: Both aromatic amino acids in pore-loop 1 are required for ATAD1's function.
source: We developed a microscopy-based assay reporting on protein mislocalization, with which we directly assessed ATAD1's activity in live cells and showed that both aromatic amino acids in pore-loop 1 are required for ATAD1's function and cannot be substituted by aliphatic amino acids.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the cell-based mislocalization assay showing that W166 and Y167 mutations to aliphatic amino acids impair function.

claim: Aromatic amino acids in pore-loop 1 cannot be substituted by aliphatic amino acids.
source: We developed a microscopy-based assay reporting on protein mislocalization, with which we directly assessed ATAD1's activity in live cells and showed that both aromatic amino acids in pore-loop 1 are required for ATAD1's function and cannot be substituted by aliphatic amino acids.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the functional assays showing that W166V, W166L, Y167V, and Y167L mutations impair ATAD1 activity.

claim: A short α-helix at the C-terminus strongly facilitates ATAD1's oligomerization.
source: A short α-helix at the C-terminus strongly facilitates ATAD1's oligomerization, a structural feature that distinguishes ATAD1 from its closely related proteins.
evidence: This is supported by structural data, SEC analysis, and functional assays showing that deletion of α11 impairs oligomerization.

claim: The α-helix at the C-terminus distinguishes ATAD1 from its closely related proteins.
source: A short α-helix at the C-terminus strongly facilitates ATAD1's oligomerization, a structural feature that distinguishes ATAD1 from its closely related proteins.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparisons showing that other AAAMC proteins have an α11-α12 organization instead of the longer α11 in ATAD1.

claim: ATAD1 has important roles in clearing out mistargeted proteins from the mitochondria.
source: ATAD1 has important roles in various biological contexts (Fresenius and Wohlever, 2019; Wang and Walter, 2020), including clearing out mistargeted proteins from the mitochondria (Chen et al., 2014; Nuebel et al., 2021; Okreglak and Walter, 2014)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: ATAD1 extracts mitochondrial precursor proteins stuck in the protein translocase channel during protein import overload.
source: ATAD1 has important roles in various biological contexts (Fresenius and Wohlever, 2019; Wang and Walter, 2020), including clearing out mistargeted proteins from the mitochondria (Chen et al., 2014; Nuebel et al., 2021; Okreglak and Walter, 2014), extracting mitochondrial precursor proteins stuck in the protein translocase channel during protein import overload (Weidberg and Amon, 2018)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Weidberg and Amon, 2018.

claim: ATAD1 mediates apoptosis by removing a BCL-family member protein.
source: ATAD1 has important roles in various biological contexts (Fresenius and Wohlever, 2019; Wang and Walter, 2020), including clearing out mistargeted proteins from the mitochondria (Chen et al., 2014; Nuebel et al., 2021; Okreglak and Walter, 2014), extracting mitochondrial precursor proteins stuck in the protein translocase channel during protein import overload (Weidberg and Amon, 2018), and mediating apoptosis by removing a BCL-family member protein (Winter et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Winter et al., 2021.

claim: ATAD1 has been implicated in the regulation of synaptic plasticity by mediating the endocytosis of neurotransmitter receptors from post-synaptic membranes.
source: In addition, ATAD1 has also been implicated in the regulation of synaptic plasticity by mediating the endocytosis of neurotransmitter receptors from post-synaptic membranes (Wang and Walter, 2020; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The removal of mistargeted tail-anchored (TA) proteins from the MOM is ATAD1's best understood function to date.
source: Among these, the removal of mistargeted tail-anchored (TA) proteins from the MOM is ATAD1's best understood function to date.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: TA proteins are integral membrane proteins that are embedded in the membrane by a hydrophobic stretch at the extreme C-terminus.
source: TA proteins are integral membrane proteins that are embedded in the membrane by a hydrophobic stretch at the extreme C-terminus.
evidence: This is a definition of TA proteins based on established knowledge.

claim: ER-targeted TA proteins are delivered to the ER membrane by the TRC proteins (Get proteins in yeast).
source: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-targeted TA proteins are delivered to the ER membrane by the TRC proteins (Get proteins in yeast) (Favaloro et al., 2008; Schuldiner et al., 2008; Stefanovic and Hegde, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: TA proteins on the MOM either insert spontaneously or are actively inserted by the mitochondrial import machinery.
source: By contrast, TA proteins on the MOM either insert spontaneously (Chio et al., 2017) or are actively inserted by the mitochondrial import machinery (Doan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The partitioning of the ER- and the mitochondria-targeted TA proteins relies on different biophysical properties of their targeting signals.
source: The partitioning of the ER- and the mitochondria-targeted TA proteins relies on different biophysical properties of their targeting signals (consisting of the transmembrane domain and the short segment C-terminal to it) (Chio et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Mistargeting of TA proteins happens in both directions between ER and mitochondria.
source: Due to a number of similarities between the ER- and mitochondria-targeted TA proteins, mistargeting happens in both directions.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by the discovery that ATAD1 can extract mislocalized TA proteins.

claim: Msp1/ATAD1 can recognize mislocalized TA proteins and extract them from mitochondria.
source: Recently, our lab and the Rutter lab independently discovered that Msp1/ATAD1 could recognize the mislocalized TA proteins and extract them from mitochondria (Chen et al., 2014; Okreglak and Walter, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to the original discovery papers.

claim: Extracted proteins are correctly inserted into the ER membrane or become degraded by the proteasome.
source: The extracted proteins are then correctly inserted into the ER membrane, from which they travel to their cognate organelle or become degraded by the proteasome (Dederer et al., 2019; Matsumoto et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: ATAD1 is a member of the AAA (ATPase Associated with diverse cellular Activities) protein family.
source: ATAD1 is a member of a large family of proteins called the AAA (ATPase Associated with diverse cellular Activities) proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge.

claim: ATAD1 is strictly conserved from yeast to humans.
source: It is strictly conserved from yeast to humans.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by the structural and functional similarities observed.

claim: Six Msp1 subunits form a helical hexamer resembling a right-handed lock-washer that surrounds the substrate in a hydrophobic central pore.
source: The structures revealed that Msp1 follows the general principle established for many AAA proteins (Gates et al., 2017; Monroe et al., 2017; de la Peña et al., 2018; Puchades et al., 2020; Puchades et al., 2017; Zehr et al., 2017): six Msp1 subunits form a helical hexamer resembling a right-handed lock-washer that surrounds the substrate in a hydrophobic central pore.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on previous structural work (Wang et al., 2020).

claim: Elements at the intersubunit interface couple ATP hydrolysis with stepwise subunit translocation to unfold the substrate peptide in the central pore.
source: Elements at the intersubunit interface couple ATP hydrolysis with stepwise subunit translocation to unfold the substrate peptide in its central pore.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on previous structural work and is a general mechanism of AAA proteins.

claim: Msp1 has an unusually hydrophobic central pore.
source: The structures also revealed elements in Msp1 that are adapted for its function of removing membrane proteins, one of which is an unusually hydrophobic central pore.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on previous structural work (Wang et al., 2020).

claim: Most AAA proteins extend only one short loop (pore-loop 1) containing a conserved aromatic amino acid to directly contact the substrate.
source: Whereas most AAA proteins extend only one short loop (pore-loop 1) containing a conserved aromatic amino acid to directly contact the substrate, Msp1 utilizes a total of three aromatic amino acids within two short loops to contact the substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on established knowledge of AAA protein structures.

claim: Msp1 utilizes a total of three aromatic amino acids within two short loops to contact the substrate.
source: Whereas most AAA proteins extend only one short loop (pore-loop 1) containing a conserved aromatic amino acid to directly contact the substrate, Msp1 utilizes a total of three aromatic amino acids within two short loops to contact the substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on previous structural work (Wang et al., 2020).

claim: The aromatic amino acids in Msp1's pore-loops enhance the bulkiness and hydrophobicity of the pore-loops, giving Msp1 a firm grip on the substrate to prevent it from backsliding.
source: We previously proposed that these aromatic amino acids enhance the bulkiness and hydrophobicity of the pore-loops, giving Msp1 a firm grip on the substrate to prevent it from backsliding, a feature that may be important for pulling hydrophobic membrane proteins out of the lipid bilayer.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed in previous work (Wang et al., 2020) and tested in the current study.

claim: The Y167A mutation impacted Msp1's activity in yeast.
source: Surprisingly, while the Y167A mutation impacted Msp1's activity, the Y167V or H206A mutation did not have a significant impact on Msp1's function.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on previous experimental results (Wang et al., 2020).

claim: The Y167V or H206A mutation did not have a significant impact on Msp1's function in yeast growth assays.
source: Surprisingly, while the Y167A mutation impacted Msp1's activity, the Y167V or H206A mutation did not have a significant impact on Msp1's function.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on previous experimental results (Wang et al., 2020).

claim: ATAD1 belongs to the 'meiotic clade' (AAAMC) within the large AAA protein family.
source: Within the large AAA protein family, ATAD1 belongs to the 'meiotic clade' (AAAMC).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Frickey and Lupas, 2004.

claim: Members of the AAAMC clade include microtubule severing proteins such as katanin and spastin, as well as Vps4.
source: Members of this clade include microtubule severing proteins such as katanin and spastin, as well as the protein that disassembles the ESCRT peptides, Vps4 (Frickey and Lupas, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Helix α12 is important in hexamer assembly and protein function for AAAMC proteins.
source: One of the unique structural elements shared by these family members is a C-terminal extension of the classic AAA protein fold, helix α12. α12 is important in hexamer assembly and protein function for AAAMC proteins (Sandate et al., 2019; Vajjhala et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The secondary structure prediction of ATAD1 shows the lack of α12 and instead predicts a longer α11.
source: The secondary structure prediction of ATAD1, however, shows the lack of α12, and instead predicts a longer α11 (the alpha helix proceeding it, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Several disease-relevant mutations are clustered around α11 in ATAD1.
source: Of note, there are several disease-relevant mutations clustered around α11, making it particularly important to understand this region in molecular detail: R9H, D221H, and E290K are found in schizophrenia patients (Umanah et al., 2017); H357Rfs*15 (a frame shift mutation resulting in a 10 amino acid extension at the C-terminus) is found in a family of patients with encephalopathy (Piard et al., 2018); and E267stop results in a truncated protein that is missing a large portion of the C-terminal domain and is found in a family of patients suffering from hypertonia, seizure, and death (Ahrens-Nicklas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: R9H, D221H, and E290K mutations are found in schizophrenia patients.
source: R9H, D221H, and E290K are found in schizophrenia patients (Umanah et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: H357Rfs*15 mutation is found in a family of patients with encephalopathy.
source: H357Rfs*15 (a frame shift mutation resulting in a 10 amino acid extension at the C-terminus) is found in a family of patients with encephalopathy (Piard et al., 2018)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: E267stop mutation is found in a family of patients suffering from hypertonia, seizure, and death.
source: E267stop results in a truncated protein that is missing a large portion of the C-terminal domain and is found in a family of patients suffering from hypertonia, seizure, and death (Ahrens-Nicklas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Density for α11 was not observed in the C.t. Msp1 structure.
source: In the C.t. Msp1 structure, we did not observe density for α11, which could be due to degradation or lack of rigid secondary structure, leaving the structure and function of α11 unresolved.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on previous structural work (Wang et al., 2020).

claim: Δ40-ATAD1E193Q formed oligomers as assessed by size exclusion chromatography.
source: Δ40-ATAD1E193Q formed oligomers as assessed by size exclusion chromatography (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 3D classification of the particles resulted in two distinct hexameric structures.
source: 3D classification of the particles resulted in two distinct hexameric structures.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a direct result of the cryo-EM data analysis.

claim: In the first structure, the six ATAD1 subunits are arranged in a right-handed spiral with an open seam between the top and the bottom subunits.
source: In the first structure, the six ATAD1 subunits (M1–M6) are arranged in a right-handed spiral with an open seam between the top and the bottom subunits (45,003 particles analyzed, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, Table 1), an arrangement resembling the 'open state' structure of Msp1 (Wang et al., 2020), as well as other related AAA proteins (Cooney et al., 2019; Han et al., 2020; Su et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2017; Twomey et al., 2019; Zehr et al., 2017; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Refinement of the open state structure resulted in a map with an average resolution of 3.7 Å.
source: Refinement of this structure resulted in a map with an average resolution of 3.7 Å.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a direct result of the cryo-EM data processing.

claim: In the second structure, M6 bridges M1 and M5, closing the hexameric ring.
source: In the second structure, the subunits are arranged in a similar fashion as the first, with the exception of M6, which is in transition to convert into M1 as part of the AAA protein functional ATPase cycle and now bridges M1 and M5, closing the hexameric ring (96,577 particles analyzed).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a direct observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The closed state structure closely resembles the 'closed state' structure observed in Msp1.
source: This structure closely resembles the 'closed state' structure observed in Msp1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Refinement of the closed state structure yielded a map with an average resolution of 3.2 Å.
source: Refinement of this structure yielded a map with an average resolution of 3.2 Å with most of the side chain densities clearly visible, which allowed us to build an atomic model.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a direct result of the cryo-EM data processing.

claim: The density of the M6 subunit in the 'closed state' structure was less well defined than the rest of the complex.
source: Noticeably, the density of the M6 subunit in the 'closed state' structure was less well defined than the rest of the complex (local resolution ranging from 4 to 6 Å, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), indicating a mixture of different states.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: A similar dynamic nature of the M6 subunit was observed in the Msp1 structure.
source: A similar dynamic nature of this subunit was also observed in the Msp1 structure (Wang et al., 2020) but the density was too poorly resolved to be interpreted.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The overall architecture of ATAD1 closely resembles that of Msp1.
source: The overall architecture of ATAD1 closely resembles that of Msp1, pointing to significant structure/function conservation throughout eukaryotic evolution.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on structural comparison.

claim: Six ATAD1 subunits rotate and translocate progressively to form a hexameric spiral assembly.
source: Six ATAD1 subunits rotate and translocate progressively to form a hexameric spiral assembly.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the cryo-EM structures.

claim: Each ATAD1 subunit consists of two subdomains, a large subdomain followed by a small subdomain.
source: Each ATAD1 subunit consists of two subdomains, a large subdomain followed by a small subdomain (Figure 1C), and the nucleotide is bound at the interface between the two.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The nucleotide is bound at the interface between the large and small subdomains.
source: Each ATAD1 subunit consists of two subdomains, a large subdomain followed by a small subdomain (Figure 1C), and the nucleotide is bound at the interface between the two.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a typical feature of AAA proteins.

claim: In the 'open state', all six subunits adopt similar overall structures.
source: In the 'open state', all six subunits adopt similar overall structures.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: To initiate subunit translocation, the M6 subunit loses its bound nucleotide and translocates upward to bridge the gap with M1.
source: To initiate the subunit translocation, the M6 subunit loses its bound nucleotide, and translocates upward to bridge the gap with M1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The small subdomain of M5 rotates toward its large subdomain during subunit translocation.
source: Meanwhile, the small subdomain of M5 rotates toward its large subdomain, allowing it to establish contacts with the small subdomain of M6 in the 'closed state' structure (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: M6 continues to move upward, assuming the M1 position in the open spiral.
source: In the next step of translocation, M6 continues to move upward, assuming the M1 position (top position) in the open spiral, detaching fully from M5, which now becomes the new M6, occupying the bottom position.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and describes the AAA protein translocation mechanism.

claim: The angle between the two subdomains of M5 widens as it reaches the M6 position.
source: Consequently, the angle between the two subdomains of M5 widens, and the subunit resumes its original conformation as it reaches the M6 position (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B, C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B, C.

claim: The hinge motion in ATAD1 argues that the two domains are connected by a flexible linker and undergo significant rotations relative to each other in a nucleotide- and subunit position-dependent manner.
source: The hinge motion in ATAD1 observed here strongly argues that the two domains are connected by a flexible linker and undergo significant rotations relative to each other in a nucleotide- and subunit position-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the structural observations.

claim: An α-helix at the extreme C-terminus of M6 points toward the core β sheet of the large subdomain of M1.
source: One structural element stood out as it was not observed previously in the C.t. Msp1 structure (Wang et al., 2020): an α-helix at the extreme C-terminus of M6 points toward the core β sheet of the large subdomain of M1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a new structural observation.

claim: Extended EM density for the C-terminal α-helix exists in other subunits as well.
source: We next asked whether this α-helix also mediates intersubunit contacts within the other subunits in the spiral. Indeed, slightly extended EM density for this α-helix exists in other subunits as well (Figures 1C and 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 1C and 2A.

claim: An α-helix (α11, amino acids 333–346) followed by a short turn (amino acids 347–351) was modeled into the density.
source: We modeled an α-helix (α11, amino acids 333–346) followed by a short turn (amino acids 347–351) into this density.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and describes the model building process.

claim: Density beyond amino acids 352–361 was not clearly visible indicating its lack of rigid structure.
source: Density beyond that (amino acids 352–361) was not clearly visible indicating its lack of rigid structure.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the cryo-EM density.

claim: A similar α-helix existed in the crystal structure of the monomeric S.c. Msp1.
source: A similar α-helix existed in the crystal structure of the monomeric S.c. Msp1 (Wohlever et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation.

claim: Six α11s form a staircase beneath pore-loop 3 in ATAD1's helical assembly.
source: In ATAD1's helical assembly, six α11s form a staircase beneath pore-loop 3, which does not contact the substrate directly but forms an interconnected network with pore-loops 1 and 2 that directly engage the substrate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: α11 lies at the interface between two adjacent subunits.
source: Zooming in on α11 reveals that it lies at the interface between two adjacent subunits (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: α11 forms extensive contacts with both the rest of the subunit and the counterclockwise adjacent subunit.
source: It forms extensive contacts with both the rest of the subunit and the counterclockwise (when viewed from the cytosol-facing side, as shown in Figure 4) adjacent subunit, bridging between the two (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: In α11M4, L336, A339, and I340 pack against the core of M4.
source: In α11M4, for example, L336, A339, and I340 pack against the core of M4 (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: M343 of α11M4 rests on the interface created by M4 and M5.
source: M343 rests on the interface created by M4 and M5
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and describes specific interactions.

claim: A349 of α11M4 points to a hydrophobic groove formed by pore-loop 3 of M5.
source: A349 points to a hydrophobic groove formed by pore-loop 3 of the M5.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and describes specific interactions.

claim: Both the side chain and the backbone carbonyl of S346 form hydrogen bonds with R254 of M5.
source: Finally, both the side chain and the backbone carbonyl of S346 form hydrogen bonds with R254 of M5 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Other AAAMC proteins such as katanin, spastin, and Vps4 are structured differently in the C-terminal region compared to ATAD1.
source: Interestingly, other AAAMC proteins such as katanin, spastin, and Vps4 are structured differently in this region (Han et al., 2020; Han et al., 2017; Sandate et al., 2019; Shin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: For katanin, spastin, and Vps4, α11 is shorter and is followed by a loop and another short helix, α12, that reaches across the intersubunit interface to contact the clockwise adjacent subunit.
source: For those proteins, α11 is shorter (consisting of three helical turns instead of four as seen in ATAD1). It is followed by a loop and another short helix, α12, that reaches across the intersubunit interface to contact the clockwise adjacent subunit (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: α12 is functionally important as its deletion impacts oligomer assembly and protein function both in vitro and in vivo.
source: α12 is functionally important as its deletion impacts oligomer assembly and protein function both in vitro and in vivo (Vajjhala et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation.

claim: Gos28 is one of ATAD1's established substrates.
source: One of ATAD1's established substrates is Gos28, a Golgi-localized TA SNARE protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on previous work.

claim: In cells lacking functional ATAD1, Gos28 localizes to mitochondria.
source: In cells lacking functional ATAD1, Gos28 localizes to mitochondria (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation.

claim: Both alleles of ATAD1 were deleted in HeLa cells using CRISPR/Cas9.
source: To analyze the activity of ATAD1 mutants in the absence of the WT enzyme, we deleted both alleles of ATAD1 in HeLa cells using CRISPR/Cas9 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In ATAD1-/- cells, a portion of EGFP-Gos28 molecules are mislocalized to mitochondria.
source: In ATAD1-/- cells, we observed two populations of Gos28 molecules: one visualized as an extended perinuclear region characteristic of the Golgi apparatus and the other in a spread-out network (Figure 3B, top row). Overlap of the EGFP signal with the signal from the mitochondria stain, MitoTracker Deep Red, showed that the latter population corresponds to the mitochondrial network, indicating that in ATAD1-/- cells, a portion of EGFP-Gos28 molecules are mislocalized to mitochondria, in line with a previous study (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Expression of WT ATAD1 in ATAD1-/- cells caused a prominent shift of EGFP-Gos28 signal toward a Golgi-like distribution.
source: We then expressed WT ATAD1 labeled with a C-terminal HaloTag in the ATAD1-/- cells (Figure 3B, middle row) and observed a prominent shift of EGFP-Gos28 signal toward a Golgi-like distribution, indicating that ATAD1 cleared mislocalized EGFP-Gos28 from the mitochondria.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Expression of ATAD1E193Q in ATAD1-/- cells mimicked the localization pattern seen in cells without ATAD1.
source: Finally, we expressed the ATAD1 bearing a mutation that inactivates its ATPase activity, ATAD1E193Q. The result mimicked the localization pattern seen in the ATAD1-/- cells (Figure 3B, top row), indicating that the ability of clearing mislocalized EGFP-Gos28 was dependent on ATAD1's enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: ATAD1-dependent removal of mistargeted Pex26 from mitochondria was observed.
source: We similarly observed ATAD1-dependent removal of mistargeted Pex26, a peroxisomal TA protein (Matsumoto et al., 2003), from mitochondria, suggesting that monitoring the clearance of a mislocalized protein is a reliable method to examine ATAD1-dependent TA protein extraction (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: A data analysis pipeline was developed using CellProfiler to quantify the degree of EGFP-Gos28 mislocalization.
source: To this end, we developed a data analysis pipeline using CellProfiler (McQuin et al., 2018; Figure 3C, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Expression of an empty vector or ATAD1E193Q in the ATAD1-/- reporter cell line led to a PCC of 0.31±0.022 and 0.31±0.017, respectively.
source: As shown in Figure 3D, expression of an empty vector or ATAD1E193Q in the ATAD1-/- reporter cell line led to a PCC of 0.31±0.022 and 0.31±0.017, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Transiently expressing WT ATAD1 showed a significantly lower PCC of 0.13±0.015 (p<0.0001).
source: By contrast, transiently expressing WT ATAD1 showed a significantly lower PCC of 0.13±0.015 (p<0.0001), confirming the visually evident changes in EFGP-Gos28 localization and validating this approach for the evaluation of functional mutants of ATAD1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ATAD1Δα11 is a truncated version of ATAD1 in which 30 amino acids at the C-terminus were deleted.
source: To this end, we made two truncated versions of ATAD1: one in which we deleted 30 amino acids at the C-terminus (removing α11 and everything C-terminal to it, ATAD1Δα11, Figure 1C)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ATAD11-351 is a truncated version of ATAD1 that keeps α11 and removes everything C-terminal to it.
source: and another in which we kept α11 and removed everything C-terminal to it (ATAD11-351, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Expression of ATAD1Δα11 in ATAD1-/- cells led to significant mislocalization of EGFP-Gos28.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, EFGP-Gos28 showed significant mislocalization to mitochondria in cells expressing ATAD1Δα11 but not ATAD11-351, suggesting that the α11 helix is required for its function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Expression of ATAD11-351 in ATAD1-/- cells did not lead to significant mislocalization of EGFP-Gos28.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, EFGP-Gos28 showed significant mislocalization to mitochondria in cells expressing ATAD1Δα11 but not ATAD11-351, suggesting that the α11 helix is required for its function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The α11 helix is required for ATAD1's function.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, EFGP-Gos28 showed significant mislocalization to mitochondria in cells expressing ATAD1Δα11 but not ATAD11-351, suggesting that the α11 helix is required for its function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the functional assay results.

claim: ATAD1Δα11 did not induce significant mislocalization of EGFP-Gos28 when expressed in WT cells.
source: By contrast, when expressed in the WT cells, ATAD1Δα11 did not induce significant mislocalization of EGFP-Gos28 (Figure 4B), indicating its recessive phenotype, that is, its lack of incorporation into and inactivating the WT hexamers present in these cells
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ATAD1Δα11 displays a recessive phenotype.
source: By contrast, when expressed in the WT cells, ATAD1Δα11 did not induce significant mislocalization of EGFP-Gos28 (Figure 4B), indicating its recessive phenotype, that is, its lack of incorporation into and inactivating the WT hexamers present in these cells
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the functional assay results.

claim: A small population of WT cells expressing ATAD1Δα11 showed EGFP-Gos28 mislocalization.
source: While expression of ATAD1Δα11 did not induce substrate mislocalization on average, it was evident by eye that a small population of WT cells expressing ATAD1Δα11 showed EGFP-Gos28 mislocalization (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: A positive correlation exists between ATAD1Δα11 expression level and the degree of Gos28 mislocalization.
source: Indeed, we observed a positive correlation between ATAD1Δα11 expression level and the degree of Gos28 mislocalization: cells that expressed more ATAD1Δα11 showed a higher degree of Gos28 mislocalization (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: α11 plays an important role in both subunit oligomerization and hexamer function.
source: These data combined showed that α11 plays an important role in both subunit oligomerization and hexamer function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the combined functional and structural data.

claim: Δ40-ATAD1Δα11 eluted exclusively as a monomer on size exclusion chromatography.
source: To this end, we purified the cytosolic domain of ATAD1 lacking the α11 helix (Δ40-ATAD1Δα11). On size exclusion, Δ40-ATAD1Δα11 eluted exclusively as a monomer.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a direct experimental observation.

claim: At similar concentrations, Δ40-ATAD1 formed oligomers on size exclusion chromatography.
source: At similar concentrations, Δ40-ATAD1 formed oligomers (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), indicating that α11 mediates oligomerization in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: α11 mediates oligomerization in vitro.
source: At similar concentrations, Δ40-ATAD1 formed oligomers (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), indicating that α11 mediates oligomerization in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the SEC data.

claim: Δ40-ATAD1Δα11 showed substantially reduced peptide-binding affinity compared to Δ40-ATAD1.
source: As expected and consistent with its inability to form hexamers, Δ40-ATAD1Δα11 also showed substantially reduced peptide-binding affinity (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The E267stop variant impacted ATAD1's function significantly.
source: Out of the variants tested, the E267stop variant impacted ATAD1's function significantly, whereas the other variants (H357Rfs*15, D221H, R9H, and E290K) displayed WT-like phenotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: H357Rfs*15, D221H, R9H, and E290K variants displayed WT-like phenotypes.
source: Out of the variants tested, the E267stop variant impacted ATAD1's function significantly, whereas the other variants (H357Rfs*15, D221H, R9H, and E290K) displayed WT-like phenotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: α11 packs against pore-loop 3 from the adjacent subunit.
source: As previously mentioned, α11 packs against pore-loop 3 from the adjacent subunit and constitutes the additional layer of the interconnected network involving three pore-loops (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Δ40-ATAD1Δα11 displays a much lower ATPase activity compared to Δ40-ATAD1.
source: As shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5, Δ40-ATAD1Δα11 displays a much lower ATPase activity compared to Δ40-ATAD1, indicating the lack of functional hexamers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: With the addition of a peptide substrate (P13), the activity of Δ40-ATAD1 is stimulated by around 41%.
source: With the addition of a peptide substrate (P13), the activity of Δ40-ATAD1 is stimulated by around 41%, whereas no significant stimulation was observed for Δ40-ATAD1Δα11 (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: No significant stimulation of ATPase activity was observed for Δ40-ATAD1Δα11 with the addition of peptide substrate.
source: With the addition of a peptide substrate (P13), the activity of Δ40-ATAD1 is stimulated by around 41%, whereas no significant stimulation was observed for Δ40-ATAD1Δα11 (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: A piece of density in the central pore resembles a linear peptide in both the closed and the open state structures.
source: Upon building all of ATAD1's amino acids into the EM density, we observed a piece of density in the central pore that resembles a linear peptide in both the closed and the open state structures.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a direct observation from the cryo-EM density.

claim: The density in the central pore likely represents a composite of peptides that co-purified with ATAD1 from E. coli.
source: This density likely represents a composite of peptides that co-purified with ATAD1 from Escherichia coli.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is an inference based on the purification method.

claim: The peptide was modeled as a 10-mer polyalanine.
source: The side chain density was clearly visible, and we modeled the peptide as a 10-mer polyalanine.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and describes the modeling approach.

claim: A peptide in the corresponding position was also observed in the Msp1 structures.
source: A peptide in the corresponding position was also observed in the Msp1 structures (Wang et al., 2020), suggesting the proteins' high affinity for their substrates.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation.

claim: Six ATAD1 subunits tightly surround the peptide in the central pore.
source: Like for Msp1, six ATAD1 subunits tightly surround the peptide in the central pore.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Amino acids used by ATAD1 to contact the substrate are phylogenetically conserved within the Msp1/ATAD1 family.
source: As summarized in the introduction, amino acids used by ATAD1 to contact the substrate are phylogenetically conserved within the Msp1/ATAD1 family, but differ from other AAA proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on sequence and structural comparisons.

claim: Six pore-loops 1 form a spiral staircase surrounding the peptide substrate.
source: Six pore-loops 1 form a spiral staircase surrounding the peptide substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Pore-loop 1 is comprised of a conserved KX1X2G motif, where X1 is a tryptophan (W166) and X2 a tyrosine (Y167).
source: Pore-loop 1 is comprised of a conserved KX1X2G motif, where X1 is a tryptophan (W166) and X2 a tyrosine (Y167).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the structure and sequence analysis.

claim: Both W166 and Y167 intercalate into the side chains of the translocating peptide.
source: Both aromatic amino acids intercalate into the side chains of the translocating peptide (Figure 1D), holding it in place.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Pore-loops 2 use a histidine (H206) to contact the backbone of the substrate.
source: Below pore-loop 1 is a second staircase formed by pore-loops 2, which use a histidine (H206) to contact the backbone of the substrate (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In most other known AAA proteins, the X1 position within pore-loop 1 is an aromatic amino acid, and the X2 position is an aliphatic amino acid that does not contact the substrate.
source: By contrast, in most other known AAA proteins, the X1 position within pore-loop 1 is an aromatic amino acid, and the X2 position is an aliphatic amino acid that does not contact the substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on established knowledge of AAA protein structures.

claim: Pore-loops 2 in most other AAA proteins usually do not contact the substrate directly.
source: Also, their pore-loops 2 usually do not contact the substrate directly.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on established knowledge of AAA protein structures.

claim: Expression of ATAD1 bearing either the W166A or Y167A mutation led to significant mislocalization of EGFP-Gos28.
source: Expression of ATAD1 bearing either the W166A (the first aromatic amino acid in pore-loop 1) or Y167A (the second aromatic amino acid in pore-loop 1) mutation led to significant mislocalization of EGFP-Gos28, suggesting that these mutations inactivate ATAD1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the cell-based assay.

claim: Expression of the aromatic mutant Y167F cleared Gos28 from mitochondria, indicating functional ATAD1.
source: By contrast, expression of the aromatic mutant Y167F cleared Gos28 from mitochondria, indicating functional ATAD1, which is consistent with what we observed for Msp1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the cell-based assay.

claim: Changing W166 or Y167 to an aliphatic amino acid impacted ATAD1's activity.
source: Interestingly, changing W166 or Y167 to an aliphatic amino impacted ATAD1's activity: ATAD1W166V, ATAD1Y167V, and ATAD1 Y167L were inactive.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the cell-based assay.

claim: ATAD1W166V, ATAD1Y167V, and ATAD1Y167L were inactive.
source: Interestingly, changing W166 or Y167 to an aliphatic amino impacted ATAD1's activity: ATAD1W166V, ATAD1Y167V, and ATAD1 Y167L were inactive.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the cell-based assay.

claim: The activity of ATAD1W166L was impacted, albeit to a lesser degree.
source: The activity of ATAD1W166L was also impacted, albeit to a lesser degree (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The aromaticity of the Y167 position is important for ATAD1 function.
source: This observation, namely that an aliphatic amino acid did not functionally replace the aromatic amino acid in this position, contrasts with our data from corresponding mutations in Msp1 in the yeast growth assay (Wang et al., 2020), suggesting either a better sensitivity of the microscopy-based assay or an inherit difference between the yeast and the mammalian system.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the functional assay results.

claim: Mutations in H206 (pore-loop 2) did not impact the function of ATAD1 in the cell-based assay.
source: We also tested the effect of mutations on H206 (pore-loop 2) in our assay. While our structural data clearly showed an interaction between H206 and the substrate backbone, mutations in this position did not impact the function of ATAD1 in this context.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the cell-based assay.

claim: ATAD1W166A, ATAD1W166V, ATAD1W166L, ATAD1Y166A, and ATAD1Y167V showed dramatically reduced (estimated >100-fold) binding to P13 compared to WT ATAD1.
source: Consistent with the cell-based assay, ATAD1W166A, ATAD1W166V, ATAD1W166L, ATAD1Y166A, and ATAD1Y167V showed dramatically reduced (estimated >100-fold) binding to P13 compared to WT ATAD1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the fluorescence polarization assay.

claim: ATAD1H206A and ATAD1Y167F showed WT-like activities in the cell-based assay, but bound P13 with much weaker affinity than the WT enzyme.
source: Both ATAD1H206A and ATAD1Y167F showed WT-like activities in the cell-based assay, but bound P13 with much weaker affinity than the WT enzyme in this assay.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on comparing the cell-based and in vitro assays.

claim: The aromaticity of the second amino acid in pore-loop 1 is important for ATAD1's function.
source: Taken together, the in vitro peptide-binding results, implications from the structure, and the cell-based assay all converge on the conclusion that the aromaticity of the second amino acid in pore-loop 1 is important for ATAD1's function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the combined experimental evidence.

claim: ATAD1's architecture fully agrees with the conserved mechanism of hand-over-hand spiral propagation established for many AAA proteins in substrate translocation.
source: Our structures show that the overall architecture of ATAD1 is very similar to that of its yeast homolog Msp1. ATAD1's architecture fully agrees with the conserved mechanism of hand-over-hand spiral propagation established for many AAA proteins in substrate translocation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the structural data.

claim: Helix α11 is required for the formation of functional oligomers.
source: We also discovered a distinct structural element, helix α11, that was present but remained structurally unresolved in Msp1, which differentiates ATAD1/Msp1 from other AAAMC proteins. Multiple lines of evidence including cell-based mislocalization, substrate binding, and ATPase activity all suggest that α11 is required for the formation of functional oligomers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the combined experimental evidence.

claim: Structural elements facing the cytosolic side of Msp1/ATAD1 (such as α11) may be evolutionarily adapted to interact with adaptors and other factors.
source: We reason that structural elements facing the cytosolic side of Msp1/ATAD1 (such as α11) may be evolutionarily adapted to interact with these factors.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is a hypothesis based on the structural observations.

claim: The α11–α12 organizational differences in different AAAMC protein subfamilies may have evolved to suit their specialized functions.
source: In this view, the α11–α12 organizational differences in different AAAMC protein subfamilies may have evolved to suit their specialized functions, such as binding to microtubules and ESCRT proteins for katanin and Vps4, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is a hypothesis based on evolutionary considerations.

claim: ATAD1/Msp1 occupy the basal position in the evolutionary tree of the AAAMC clade.
source: This view is supported by the fact that ATAD1/Msp1 occupy the basal position in the evolutionary tree of this clade, and the other members (katanin, spastin, and Vps4) share a common evolutionary ancestor (Frickey and Lupas, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation.

claim: The flat, bulkier pore-loop amino acids give AAA proteins a stronger grip, with higher coupling efficiency between ATP hydrolysis and substrate unfolding.
source: A study on the bacterial AAA proteins ClpXP (Rodriguez-Aliaga et al., 2016), for example, showed that the flat, bulkier pore-loop amino acids give the protein a stronger grip, that is higher coupling efficiency between ATP hydrolysis and substrate unfolding, yet are compromised in the rate of substrate translocation (measured as protein unfolding with ClpXP).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation.

claim: Having a tighter grip on the substrate may be important for ATAD1's function of extracting hydrophobic membrane proteins from the lipid membrane.
source: Given ATAD1's function is to extract hydrophobic membrane proteins from the lipid membrane, having a tighter grip on the substrate may be important, even if it comes at the cost of a slower translocation speed.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is a hypothesis based on the functional requirements.

claim: Cdc48 possesses two aromatic amino acids in its pore-loop 1.
source: Similar to ATAD1, Cdc48, a protein that removes misfolded membrane proteins from the ER membrane, also possesses two aromatic amino acids in its pore-loop 1 (Cooney et al., 2019; Twomey et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: The additional aromatic amino acids in the central pore evolved to aid in the removal of membrane proteins.
source: Similar to ATAD1, Cdc48, a protein that removes misfolded membrane proteins from the ER membrane, also possesses two aromatic amino acids in its pore-loop 1 (Cooney et al., 2019; Twomey et al., 2019), suggesting that the additional aromatic amino acids in the central pore evolved to aid in the removal of membrane proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is a hypothesis based on comparative analysis.

claim: ATAD1/Msp1 utilize a conceptually similar mechanism for substrate translocation as many other AAA proteins.
source: To conclude, while ATAD1/Msp1 utilize a conceptually similar mechanism for substrate translocation as many other AAA proteins, the high conservation of several unique features between ATAD1 and Msp1 suggests that evolution fine-tuned these enzymes early in eukaryotic cell evolution for their special role in membrane protein extraction and protein quality control.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the structural and functional data.

claim: Evolution fine-tuned ATAD1/Msp1 early in eukaryotic cell evolution for their special role in membrane protein extraction and protein quality control.
source: To conclude, while ATAD1/Msp1 utilize a conceptually similar mechanism for substrate translocation as many other AAA proteins, the high conservation of several unique features between ATAD1 and Msp1 suggests that evolution fine-tuned these enzymes early in eukaryotic cell evolution for their special role in membrane protein extraction and protein quality control.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the evolutionary conservation observed.
